episodes.title: That Wobbly Tape Measure Hook Is Not Broken
episodes.notes: Payoff is the 1/16-inch sliding compensation (US patent 4466194, 'True zero tape hook'). Never spoken.
episodes.content: The metal hook on the end of a tape measure wobbles, and every time you notice it you assume the thing is worn out. The hook is supposed to move. It slides exactly as far as the hook is thick, about a sixteenth of an inch. Hook it over the edge of a board and it pulls out, adding that thickness back. Push it into a corner and it slides in, taking that thickness away. Either way the tape starts reading from true zero. The loosest part of the tool is the part keeping it honest.

episodes.title: What The Black Dots Around Your Windshield Are Doing
episodes.notes: Frit band = ceramic enamel baked into glass. Dots are the thermal gradient. Never spoken.
episodes.content: Look along the top edge of a windshield and you'll find a black border that breaks into a scatter of dots before it fades out. That border is ceramic paint baked into the glass, and it is covering the adhesive that holds the windshield onto the car. Sunlight would slowly cook that glue, so the black band shields it. The dots are the clever part. Black glass heats faster than clear glass, and a hard edge between the two would build enough stress to crack the pane, so the dots spread that change out gradually.

episodes.title: Your Quarter Is Still Protecting Silver It Doesn't Have
episodes.notes: Reeding as anti-clipping. Newton was Warden of the Royal Mint from 1696. Never spoken.
episodes.content: Run your thumb around the edge of a quarter and you'll feel ridges, which is a strange thing to put on a coin containing nothing worth stealing. Back when coins were actually silver, people shaved slivers off the rims, spent the coin anyway, and kept the shavings. A shaved coin looked almost normal. So mints cut grooves into the edge, and a shaved coin stopped looking normal immediately, because the pattern just ended. Isaac Newton used it against clippers as warden of the Royal Mint. The silver is long gone. The ridges stayed.

episodes.title: The Shiny Side Of Foil Is A Manufacturing Accident
episodes.notes: Two sheets milled together in the final pass. Neither side performs differently. Never spoken.
episodes.content: One side of aluminum foil is shiny and the other side is dull, and the box never explains why. It is not a coating, and it is not a nonstick side. Foil gets rolled thinner and thinner between polished steel rollers, and by the last pass it is so thin a single sheet would tear itself apart, so the mill runs two sheets through stacked together. The outer faces press against mirror-bright steel and come out shiny. The two inner faces press against each other and come out dull.

episodes.title: The Bumpy Tiles On The Sidewalk Are A Two-Word Language
episodes.notes: Seiichi Miyake, Okayama, 1965, self-funded. Domes = warning, bars = guidance. Never spoken.
episodes.content: Those bumpy tiles at the edge of a train platform are a language, and it only has two words. Round domes mean stop, because there is an edge, a road, or a drop ahead. Long parallel bars mean keep going, this way is safe. Both are readable through a shoe or the tip of a cane, and the yellow helps if you still have some sight. An engineer in Japan named Seiichi Miyake paid for the first ones himself in 1965, because a friend was going blind. They are under most of the world's feet now.

episodes.title: Planes Still Have Ashtrays And It's Not An Oversight
episodes.notes: FAA minimum equipment. Fire risk of a cigarette in a paper waste bin. Never spoken.
episodes.content: Smoking has been banned on flights for decades, and there is still an ashtray built into the airplane bathroom door. It is not a leftover nobody removed. Regulators require it, and a plane can be held on the ground over a broken one. The reasoning is bleak and completely correct. Somebody is eventually going to smoke in there anyway, and the only question is where the cigarette ends up. Without an ashtray, it goes in the bin, on top of the paper towels. It is not there for smokers.

episodes.title: Why Cars Got A Third Brake Light
episodes.notes: CHMSL, mandated US 1986. Early trials suggested ~35%; long-run effectiveness ~4.3%. Both reported honestly.
episodes.content: Somewhere in the back window of every car sits a third brake light, higher and more centered than the other two. It exists because the original pair are easy to misread. They sit low, they sit far apart, and they are right beside tail lights that are already glowing. A single light up high, dark until the driver brakes, cannot be confused with anything. Early taxi-fleet trials suggested a third fewer rear-end collisions. Once every car had one the real figure settled nearer four percent, which is still tens of thousands of crashes a year.

episodes.title: Sneakers Come With An Anti-Blister Setting
episodes.notes: The extra eyelet enables a heel lock / runner's loop. Stops heel lift, which causes friction blisters.
episodes.content: Almost every sneaker has one extra lace hole at the top that nobody uses, set slightly back from the rest. Thread the lace through it on each side and you get a small loop above the ankle. Cross the laces into the opposite loop, pull, and the collar clamps down around your ankle instead of squeezing the middle of your foot. Your heel stops lifting out of the shoe with every step. Heel lift is what rubs a blister into the back of your foot on a long walk.

episodes.title: The Hole In A Padlock Lets Water Out, Not In
episodes.notes: Drainage first, lubrication access second. Never spoken.
episodes.content: Flip a padlock over and there is a small hole in the bottom of it, which looks like an excellent way to let water into an expensive lock. It does the opposite. A padlock left outdoors collects moisture no matter what you do, from rain, from washing, from the air itself. Sealed shut, that water sits on steel springs and pins until they rust into a solid lump, or freeze there overnight. The hole lets it fall straight back out. It also gives you somewhere to put a drop of oil.

episodes.title: Charger Cables Have A Lump That Stops Them Broadcasting
episodes.notes: Ferrite bead / choke. High-frequency EMI absorbed and dissipated as heat. Never spoken.
episodes.content: There is a hard lump molded around your laptop charger cable, and it is surprisingly heavy for its size. Inside it is a ring of ferrite, an iron-based ceramic. A power cable is a long piece of wire, and a long piece of wire is an antenna, so it picks up and radiates high-frequency noise it was never meant to carry. The ferrite ring lets your actual power pass straight through, and turns that noise into a tiny amount of heat. It is a filter wrapped around a cable, stopping your charger from transmitting.

episodes.title: A Brick Has Holes For Three Different Reasons
episodes.notes: Mortar key, even drying/firing, less clay and weight. Never spoken.
episodes.content: A brick has holes punched straight through the middle, which is an odd thing to do to an object whose whole job is being solid. The holes make it better. Mortar squeezes down into them and sets there, so each brick is keyed into the one above rather than glued along a flat face. Wet clay also has to dry and fire without cracking, and heat reaches the middle of a perforated brick far faster than a solid lump. Less clay, less fuel, lighter to lift, stronger wall.

episodes.title: That Gravel Under Train Tracks Isn't Landscaping
episodes.notes: Load spreading, lateral restraint via angular interlock, drainage, vibration damping.
episodes.content: Train tracks sit on a bed of sharp, angular gravel, and it is there on purpose. A loaded train puts enormous weight onto a thin steel rail, and the stones spread that load sideways so the ground underneath does not sink. Because they are angular rather than rounded, they lock against each other and stop the track creeping out of line. Rain drains through the gaps instead of turning the bed to mud. And the layer soaks up vibration, which is why a passing train shakes the ground less than it should.

episodes.title: Chip Bags Are Not Filled With Air
episodes.notes: Nitrogen flush, oxygen under 3%, plus slack fill as transit cushion. Never spoken.
episodes.content: A bag of chips is mostly not chips, and the empty part is not air. Air is a fifth oxygen, and oxygen turns the oil in a chip rancid within days. So the bag gets flushed with nitrogen, which is inert and does nothing to food, and the oxygen inside drops to almost nothing. That is the freshness half. The other half is that chips are fragile and get stacked, dropped and driven across a country, so the gas is also a pillow. You are buying a cushion that doubles as a preservative.

episodes.title: Public Toilet Seats Have That Gap Because Of A Rulebook
episodes.notes: Open-front seats: ASNPC 1955, Uniform Plumbing Code since 1973. Codes, not federal law.
episodes.content: Public toilet seats have a gap at the front, and the one in your house almost certainly does not. It is written down. The plumbing codes most of the country builds to call for open-front seats in public restrooms, and have for over fifty years. The gap keeps the seat clear of the area you are most likely to touch while wiping, which matters far more when hundreds of strangers share one seat. It also leaves urine nowhere to pool. What reads as cost-cutting is a rule.

episodes.title: Why Soda Cans Get Narrower At The Top
episodes.notes: Lid metal is far thicker than wall metal; shrinking lid diameter saves disproportionate aluminum.
episodes.content: The top of a soda can is visibly narrower than the rest of it, tapering inward just before the lid. That taper is not shaped for your mouth. The lid has to be much thicker than the walls, because it holds the pressure and carries a tab you can tear open with one finger. Thick metal is expensive metal, so shrinking the lid saves far more aluminum than shaving the sides ever could. Six millimeters have come off it since the sixties, saving close to two hundred million pounds a year.

episodes.title: A Revolving Door Is Solving A Problem You Can't See
episodes.notes: Stack effect. Patented 1888, Theophilus Van Kannel, Philadelphia. Never spoken.
episodes.content: A revolving door is slower than a normal door, more expensive to build, and much harder to carry anything through, and tall buildings keep installing them anyway. Warm air inside a tall building rises and escapes out of the top, and that pulls cold air in hard at street level. On an ordinary door, that pressure difference turns the entrance into a wind tunnel and throws the heating out into the street. A revolving door never actually opens. Only the wedge of air in your compartment travels with you.

episodes.title: Why One Of Your Car Mirrors Comes With A Warning
episodes.notes: FMVSS 111: US driver-side must be flat unit-magnification; passenger side may be convex, and must carry the warning.
episodes.content: On an American car the passenger side mirror is curved, the driver's side one is flat, and only the curved one carries a warning printed on the glass. Curving a mirror squeezes a wider slice of road into the same piece of glass, which is how it covers a blind spot a flat mirror cannot reach. The price is that everything in it looks smaller, and your brain reads smaller as further away. The warning exists because the mirror really is misleading you, and someone decided that had to be admitted in writing.

episodes.title: Light Turns Beer Into Something Close To Skunk Spray
episodes.notes: Riboflavin photosensitizes; isohumulones break down to a thiol chemically near skunk spray. Brown blocks ~98%.
episodes.content: Beer almost always comes in brown glass, because light physically breaks beer. Hops leave compounds in the liquid that are stable in the dark. Hit them with blue and ultraviolet light, and riboflavin, a vitamin already in the beer, acts as a middleman. It absorbs the light and hands the energy along until those hop compounds shatter into something chemically close to skunk spray. That is not a figure of speech. Brown glass blocks nearly all of those wavelengths. Green blocks a fraction, which is why some imports taste faintly like a warning.

episodes.title: Why The Cabin Lights Go Down Before Landing
episodes.notes: Dark adaptation takes minutes; takeoff and landing are the highest-risk evacuation windows.
episodes.content: The cabin lights go down before a night landing, and it reads as mood lighting or saving power. It is neither. Eyes take several minutes to adapt to darkness, and takeoff and landing are when an evacuation is most likely to be needed. If the cabin were brightly lit and the power went, everyone aboard would be effectively blind at the worst possible moment. Dimming early means your eyes are already adjusted, and the floor path lighting reads clearly instead of washing out. The lights go down so you can see.

episodes.title: Your Receipt Was Never Printed With Ink
episodes.notes: Leuco dye + developer in a surface coating; reaction is not permanent. Never spoken.
episodes.content: A receipt left in a wallet slowly goes blank, because there was never any ink on it. Receipt paper is coated with a colorless dye and a chemical developer sitting right next to each other, doing nothing. The printer has no ink and no ribbon. It has a row of tiny heaters. Wherever it touches, the coating melts, the two chemicals meet, and that spot turns black. The catch is the reaction never locks. Heat off a dashboard or friction in a back pocket keeps driving it until the text vanishes.
